analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run public health insurance plan to compete with private insurers.
analysis.headline: The public option bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a Consumer Choice Health Plan run by a new office inside the Department of Health and Human Services, offering coverage to anyone eligible to buy insurance through a national insurance exchange [S2]. It would pay doctors and hospitals at Medicare rates at first, require providers in Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP to see Plan enrollees for at least three years, and require the Plan to pay back its startup funding and become financially self-sustaining on premiums [S3]. To fund oversight of insurance plans, it would also charge a fee on every health insurance policy and self-insured health plan [S2]. The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Individuals and employers eligible to buy coverage through the exchange could enroll in a government-run plan intended to be affordable and to hold private insurers' prices and practices in check; the bill's own findings state that a competing public plan is the way to guarantee affordable, adequate, accountable coverage [S3]. Consumers would also gain detailed standardized disclosures of what plans cover and cost [S3], and independent letter-grade rankings of every plan in the exchange published by a new consumer-majority nonprofit trust [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Creates a public health insurance plan available to all individuals eligible to buy coverage through the exchange, with enrollment counting toward any federal insurance mandate [S2].
Requires the Plan to pay providers at Medicare rates for its first two years, a benchmark generally below what private plans pay, and lets the Director adjust rates to keep access adequate [S3].
Forces Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP providers to accept Plan enrollees for at least three years, guaranteeing Plan customers a broad provider network from day one [S3].

Establishes a nonprofit America's Health Insurance Trust with a majority of consumer representatives on its board to grade every exchange plan from A to F on affordability, claims handling, and complaints, with data plans must hand over [S3].

Mandates standardized definitions and public disclosure of policy language, claims-payment practices, loss ratios, exclusions, and simulated patient cost scenarios for conditions like maternity care, cancer, and diabetes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers would face a government-run competitor. Every health insurance policy and self-insured employer plan would pay a per-person fee ($0.50 per covered life in 2010-2013, $1 after, indexed to health spending growth) to fund the oversight trust [S3]. Providers would initially be paid Medicare rates for Plan patients, and the Treasury general fund would advance three years of startup funding that the Plan must repay [S3].

drawbacks.text: The Plan would rely on three years of Treasury general-fund transfers to get started and must repay them; if it went insolvent, supplemental funding would need a three-fifths supermajority vote of both chambers, raising the risk that the Plan could fail financially [S3].
The new fee on every health insurance policy and self-insured plan would be paid by insurers and plan sponsors, and could be passed through to premiums and employer costs [S3].

Requiring Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP providers to take Plan patients at Medicare rates for three years would hold reimbursement below what private plans generally pay, an obligation hospitals and physicians could object to even with the opt-out and capacity exceptions [S3].

The Plan's eligibility is defined entirely by the National Health Insurance Exchange, which the bill itself notes has not been established, so the whole structure depends on other legislation creating the exchange first [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — a government-run plan whose Medicare-anchored payment rates would pressure private insurers' premiums — is real and large for anyone buying individual or small-group coverage. The costs are serious but manageable by design: the bill builds in repayment of startup funds, a 5 percent cap on administrative spending, a contingency reserve, and annual GAO audits, which makes the insolvency risk a genuine but hedged concern. The fee on all health plans and the forced provider participation at Medicare rates are the parts an honest supporter would have had to defend hardest.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on June 17, 2009 and referred the same day to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when that Congress ended in January 2011 [S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Rockefeller introduced the Consumers Health Care Act of 2009 with Sen. Brown on June 17, 2009; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — and the bill expired with the 111th Congress [S5].

The public insurance option it proposed was never enacted; the national exchange it depended on was never established, and the United States went on to pass health reform without a government-run public plan competing with private insurers [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers are better off because the bill died: no government-run plan ever entered the market to compete on price with them, and the exchange-based public option was dropped from health reform. Providers also avoided the three-year obligation to take Plan patients at Medicare rates.

for.name: Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV
for.role: Senator from West Virginia; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor on June 17, 2009 [S5].

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Joined Rockefeller in introducing the bill at introduction [S3].

against.name: Sen. Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup in the Finance Committee; no committee action of any kind was taken during the bill's 19 months in the committee's custody [S5].

against.name: America's Health Insurance Plans and the health insurance industry
against.role: Health insurance industry trade association and insurers
against.what_they_did: Ran a well-documented public and lobbying campaign against a government-run public insurance option during the 2009 health reform debate.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a Democratic-only proposal — both the sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican supported it at any point [S4].

industries.note: The bill would put a government-run plan paying Medicare-anchored rates directly into competition with private insurers on the same exchange, and require insurers to hand sensitive underwriting, rescission, and claims data to a consumer-majority oversight trust. Insurers' interest in stopping it ran against the affordability interests of the people who buy their policies.

Employers that self-insure or buy group policies would pay a per-life fee ($0.50 in 2010-2013, $1 after, indexed to health spending) to fund the oversight trust, and could buy the public Plan for their workers, which could reshape employer coverage.

Providers would be required to accept Plan patients for at least three years at Medicare rates, generally below private payment levels, which protects Plan enrollees' access but lowers provider revenue; after three years they could opt out.
